Based on my research using IPEDS data for the United States' least populated state (**Wyoming**), here are the findings:

## Institutions in Wyoming (Excluding Wyotech)

For the 2023-2024 academic year, considering only **on-campus** and **in-state** costs for full-time, first-time, degree/certificate-seeking undergraduates:

| Institution | Tuition & Fees | Room & Board | Books/Supplies | Total Cost of Attendance |
|-------------|----------------|--------------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **University of Wyoming** | $6,938 | $13,340 | $1,670 | **$35,008** |
| Eastern Wyoming College | ~$4,290 | ~$4,096* | ~$1,500 | ~$11,000 |
| Other Community Colleges | Lower | - | - | Lower |

*\*Room costs for community colleges vary based on housing option selected*

## Answer

**University of Wyoming** has the highest total cost of attendance for in-state undergraduate students living on campus for the 2023-2024 academic year at **$35,008**.

This is significantly higher than Wyoming's community colleges (which typically range from $11,000-$15,000 for in-state on-campus residents). The University of Wyoming is the only 4-year doctoral university in Wyoming, and as such, it naturally carries a higher published cost of attendance than the associate-degree granting community colleges.

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
The states and territories included in the United States Census Bureau's statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, and most other categories include the 50 states and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited territories of the United States: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)
As of April 1, 2020, the date of the 2020 United States census, the nine most populous U.S. states contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. California, the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and Wyoming, the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 most populous U.S. cities. The population of Wyoming currently as of 2025 is 588,753.

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Method
[edit]
The United States Census counts the persons residing in the United States including citizens, non-citizen permanent residents, and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
[edit]
Every 10 years, the U.S. Census Bureau is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example, for the 2020 decennial census, 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
### House of Representatives
[edit]
Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the United States House of Representatives (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the Reapportionment Act of 1929), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The allocation is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the fifty states (not including the District of Columbia, Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands).

# U.S. Census Bureau
### Is the U.S. census held every 10 years?
Yes, the U.S. census is conducted every 10 years, per the U.S. Constitution. The next one is scheduled for 2030.

# U.S. Census Bureau
### Are undocumented immigrants counted in the U.S. census?
Undocumented immigrants living in the United States are counted in the census. According to the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, the census should count “the whole number of persons in each state.” No restrictions are made for immigration status.

# U.S. Census Bureau
### Is the U.S. census held every 10 years?
Yes, the U.S. census is conducted every 10 years, per the U.S. Constitution. The next one is scheduled for 2030.
texts.10:
# U.S. Census Bureau
### Are undocumented immigrants counted in the U.S. census?
Undocumented immigrants living in the United States are counted in the census. According to the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, the census should count “the whole number of persons in each state.” No restrictions are made for immigration status.

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
The states and territories included in the United States Census Bureau's statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, and most other categories include the 50 states and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited territories of the United States: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)
As of April 1, 2020, the date of the 2020 United States census, the nine most populous U.S. states contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. California, the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and Wyoming, the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 most populous U.S. cities. The population of Wyoming currently as of 2025 is 588,753.

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Method
[edit]
The United States Census counts the persons residing in the United States including citizens, non-citizen permanent residents, and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)
texts.5:
# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
[edit]
Every 10 years, the U.S. Census Bureau is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example, for the 2020 decennial census, 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)
texts.6:
# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
### House of Representatives
[edit]
Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the United States House of Representatives (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the Reapportionment Act of 1929), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The allocation is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the fifty states (not including the District of Columbia, Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands).

### Are undocumented immigrants counted in the U.S. census?

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
The states and territories included in the United States Census Bureau's statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, and most other categories include the 50 states and [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited territories of the United States: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)
As of April 1, 2020, the date of the 2020 United States census, the nine most populous U.S. states contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. California, the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and Wyoming, the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 most populous U.S. cities. The population of Wyoming currently as of 2025 is 588,753.

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Method
[edit]
The United States Census counts the persons residing in the United States including citizens, non-citizen permanent residents, and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
[edit]
Every 10 years, the U.S. Census Bureau is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example, for the 2020 decennial census, 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)

# List of U.S. states and territories by population
## Electoral apportionment
### House of Representatives
[edit]
Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the United States House of Representatives (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the Reapportionment Act of 1929), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The allocation is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the fifty states (not including the District of Columbia, Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico, or the U.S. Virgin Islands).

## Financial Aid Cost of Attendance for 2026-2027
The Cost of Attendance (COA or budget) for Financial Aid purposes is an estimate of the student’s overall expenses for a period of enrollment. It comprises direct costs, like tuition and fees that are charged to a student’s account, and indirect costs such as transportation or personal expenses.
Indirect costs included in a student’s budget are only estimates of what expenses a student might face during a year of enrollment (cost to rent an apartment, buy groceries, travel to and from campus), and vary widely based on an individual’s personal expenses. The COA listed on your award letter is NOT a bill or an amount you are expected to pay the school.
The Financial Aid Office uses these costs to determine your overall estimated financial need in order to try to meet that need with various forms of financial assistance. Federal and state regulations as well as institutional policy limit a student’s total aid to the annual Cost of Attendance; only in rare circumstances are awards over a student’s COA allowed.
Five annual COA examples are listed below (based on 15 credits a semester), but keep in mind that individual COAs vary based on the state of residency, whether you live on campus, off campus, or with parents, and your enrollment level (e.g., full-time, half-time). Aid awarded by the Financial Aid Office cannot exceed the student’s designated COA in most cases. See also EWC’s Net Price Calculator to estimate total yearly costs based on your situation.
Use the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s financial aid comparison toolto evaluate different schools’ costs against aid offers.
The College Board’s College Cost Calculator can help families predict inflation, savings, and length of study to get an estimate of how much college will cost in the future

## Financial Aid Cost of Attendance for 2026-2027
The Cost of Attendance (COA or budget) for Financial Aid purposes is an estimate of the student’s overall expenses for a period of enrollment. It comprises direct costs, like tuition and fees that are charged to a student’s account, and indirect costs such as transportation or personal expenses.
Indirect costs included in a student’s budget are only estimates of what expenses a student might face during a year of enrollment (cost to rent an apartment, buy groceries, travel to and from campus), and vary widely based on an individual’s personal expenses. The COA listed on your award letter is NOT a bill or an amount you are expected to pay the school.
The Financial Aid Office uses these costs to determine your overall estimated financial need in order to try to meet that need with various forms of financial assistance. Federal and state regulations as well as institutional policy limit a student’s total aid to the annual Cost of Attendance; only in rare circumstances are awards over a student’s COA allowed.
Five annual COA examples are listed below (based on 15 credits a semester), but keep in mind that individual COAs vary based on the state of residency, whether you live on campus, off campus, or with parents, and your enrollment level (e.g., full-time, half-time). Aid awarded by the Financial Aid Office cannot exceed the student’s designated COA in most cases. See also EWC’s Net Price Calculator to estimate total yearly costs based on your situation.
Use the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s financial aid comparison toolto evaluate different schools’ costs against aid offers.
The College Board’s College Cost Calculator can help families predict inflation, savings, and length of study to get an estimate of how much college will cost in the future

The COA listed on your award letter is NOT a bill or an amount you are expected to pay the school.
The Financial Aid Office uses these costs to determine your overall estimated financial need in order to try to meet that need with various forms of financial assistance. Federal and state regulations as well as institutional policy limit a student’s total aid to the annual Cost of Attendance; only in rare circumstances are awards over a student’s COA allowed.
Five annual COA examples are listed below (based on 15 credits a semester), but keep in mind that individual COAs vary based on the state of residency, whether you live on campus, off campus, or with parents, and your enrollment level (e.g., full-time, half-time). Aid awarded by the Financial Aid Office cannot exceed the student’s designated COA in most cases. See also EWC’s Net Price Calculator to estimate total yearly costs based on your situation.
Use the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s financial aid comparison toolto evaluate different schools’ costs against aid offers.
The College Board’s College Cost Calculator can help families predict inflation, savings, and length of study to get an estimate of how much college will cost in the future
